title: Your first mesh
text: This tutorial generates a small refined quad mesh from shapely geometries, looks at it, checks it and writes it as a UGRID net file.

title: Your first mesh
text:
The input
A mesh needs a domain, the area it covers, and a base cell, the size of its coarsest squares. Refinement areas say where the mesh must be finer: each is a polygon paired with a refinement level, the number of times the base cell is halved there. Coordinates are in RD New (EPSG:28992).

from shapely import Point, box

domain = box(155_000, 463_000, 155_640, 463_480)
refinement_areas = [
    (Point(155_250, 463_240).buffer(60), 2),  # 32 m / 2**2 = 8 m cells
    (box(155_450, 463_080, 155_600, 463_160), 1),  # 16 m cells
]

title: Your first mesh
text:
Generate

from refined_quads import generate

mesh = generate(
    domain,
    cell_size=32.0,
    refinement_areas=refinement_areas,
    transition_rows=[1, 1],
    crs="EPSG:28992",
)
print(mesh)

Mesh(nodes=844, faces=916, cell_size=32, levels=2, crs=EPSG:28992)


transition_rows gives, per step from coarse to fine, how many rows of finer cells surround a finer area before the mesh coarsens. Here one row for the step from 32 m to 16 m and one for 16 m to 8 m.

title: refine
text:
refine(
    mesh,
    refinement_areas,
    *,
    transition_rows=1,
    domain=None,
    water_areas=(),
    water_removal='centre',
    crs=None,
    progress=None,
)
Refine an existing mesh locally with new refinement areas.
The lattice and the lattice squares are recognised from the cells of the mesh (transition cells as parts of their square), the new areas are applied, the 2:1 balance is restored where needed and the transitions around the changed squares are rebuilt. Squares that do not change keep their cells exactly, nodes included.

title: API reference
text:
Everything public is available from the top-level package refined_quads.



generate
Generate a refined quad mesh over a domain.


refine
Refine an existing mesh locally with new refinement areas.


check
Check a mesh for hanging nodes, 2:1 balance, FM orthogonality and orientation.


MeshReport
Result of :func:check.









Mesh
An immutable refined quad mesh.


Lattice
The fixed grid of points on which every square of a refined quad mesh has its corners.


RefineResult
The result of :func:refine.


ReplacementMap
What a refine did to the cells of the existing mesh.









read_domain
Read the domain from a GIS layer; its polygons are merged into one.


read_refinement_areas
Read refinement areas from a GIS layer.


read_water_areas
Read water areas from a GIS layer.


Areas
Polygons with their coordinate reference system.









read_ugrid
Read the 2D mesh of a UGRID netCDF file.


write_ugrid
Write a mesh as a UGRID-1.0 netCDF file that D-HYDRO and D-Flow FM read.









MeshSpec
Everything refined-quads generate needs; one-to-one with the TOML file.


RefineSpec
Everything refined-quads refine needs besides the mesh; one-to-one with the TOML.


LayerSource
A layer of a GeoPackage or shapefile.


RefinementSource
A layer with refinement areas.









InputError
Invalid input: the package raises this instead of silently adjusting the input.


Cancelled
The run was cancelled through the progress callback.


MeshRecognitionError
An existing mesh is not a refined quad mesh this package can refine.


OrthogonalityRepairError
The orthogonality repair could not make every internal edge FM-orthogonal.






Exit codes 0 success, 1 the run failed, 2 invalid input or arguments.

title: refined-quads
text:
What it does

Generate a mesh over a domain with refinement areas, transition rows and water areas, in Python or from a TOML file on the command line.
Refine an existing mesh — also one made by another program — with new refinement areas, without its original input; cells that do not change stay exactly as they are.
Check a mesh for the properties D-Flow FM and refining rely on: no hanging nodes, 2:1 balance and FM orthogonality.
Read and write UGRID net files that D-HYDRO and D-Flow FM use.

title: refined-quads
text:
Install
The package is not on PyPI yet. Install it from the repository with uv:
uv add "refined-quads @ git+https://github.com/HKV-products-services/refined-quads"
Its dependencies (numpy, shapely, netCDF4, pyogrio, pyproj and meshkernel) all come as wheels; no separate GDAL installation is needed. On macOS the meshkernel wheel needs OpenMP from Homebrew (brew install libomp); the package is tested on Windows and Linux.

Your first mesh walks through generating, checking and writing a mesh.

title: Read layers from a GeoPackage
text:
Rules

Layer name. A file with one layer needs no name; with several layers the name is required, otherwise you get an error that lists the layers.
Level. level is the name of a column with the refinement level per polygon, or one integer for the whole layer (level=3). A missing or invalid level (0, a negative number, 2.5, empty) raises an error that names the feature.
Domain. All polygons of the domain layer are merged into one (multi)polygon.
CRS. The mesh gets the CRS of the domain. Other layers are transformed to it. A layer without CRS raises an error unless you pass crs= for it; a geographic CRS (degrees) for the domain raises an error, as cell sizes must be in metres.
GeoDataFrame. Instead of a path you may pass a GeoDataFrame (or any object with geometry and crs attributes): read_refinement_areas(frame, level="refinement").
Shapely geometries. Plain shapely geometries have no CRS: pass crs= to generate (see the tutorial).

title: Refined quad meshes
text: A refined quad mesh is a 2D mesh of axis-aligned squares on a fixed lattice, locally refined by repeated halving, with triangles only where cell sizes change.

title: Refined quad meshes
section: Base cell, refinement level and lattice
text:
Base cell, refinement level and lattice
The base cell is the coarsest square; its size is any positive length, for example 32 m or 25 m. Each refinement level halves it once: level 0 is the base cell, level L has side cell size / 2**L. A 25 m base cell gives 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 m cells at levels 1 to 3.
The lattice is the fixed grid of points on which every square has its corners: an origin and the base cell. By default the origin is the lower-left corner of the domain rounded down to a multiple of the base cell, so meshes with the same base cell line up. Internally every corner is an integer index on the finest level of the lattice, so coordinates are computed once, as origin + index * unit, and comparisons are exact.
A lattice square is a square of the quadtree: a base cell or one of the squares its halving gives. It becomes one square cell, or is filled by transition cells.

Neighbouring lattice squares differ at most one level (2:1 balance). Where a finer square meets a coarser one, the coarser square gets a node in the middle of that side and is split into transition cells: one split side gives a fan of three triangles, two adjacent split sides four triangles, and two opposite or three or four split sides four squares around the centre. Together they fill the lattice square exactly, so there are no hanging nodes (nodes in the middle of another cell’s edge).

title: Refined quad meshes
text:
Domain and water
The domain encloses the mesh. A lattice square that overlaps it is kept whole, so the outer edge follows the lattice rather than the polygon exactly. Water areas and holes in the domain are clipped out of the finished mesh cell by cell (see Water areas); after that some lattice squares are filled only partly, which is how the remaining cells follow the water’s edge.

title: FM orthogonality
text: D-Flow FM computes the flow between two cells along the line that joins their centres. That works well when the line crosses their shared edge at a right angle; D-Flow FM rejects a network (“network is not orthogonal”) where it does not.

title: FM orthogonality
text:
The measure
For every internal edge (an edge of exactly two cells):
orth_e = | cos(angle between the edge and the line joining the two cell centres) |
0 is perfectly orthogonal and 1 the worst; an edge is acceptable when orth_e <= 0.30. The centre of a triangle is its circumcentre clipped into the triangle (the RGFGRID centre), the centre of any other cell the mean of its nodes. Clipping matters: the raw circumcentre of an obtuse sliver lies far outside it, on the perpendicular bisector of every edge, which would hide exactly the slivers D-Flow FM rejects. This is the measure of the D-HYDRO mesh editor; check reports it per edge.

from shapely import Point, box

from refined_quads import check, generate

mesh = generate(
    box(155_000, 463_000, 155_320, 463_240),
    cell_size=32.0,
    refinement_areas=[(Point(155_160, 463_120).buffer(40), 2)],
    transition_rows=[1, 1],
    crs="EPSG:28992",
)
report = check(mesh)
print(f"{report.orthogonality.size} internal edges, worst orth_e = {report.max_orthogonality:.3f}")

653 internal edges, worst orth_e = 0.000

title: FM orthogonality
text:
Repair
The transition patterns are orthogonal by construction. Later steps (the head-to-toe correction of neighbouring transition squares, resolving hanging nodes) can still leave a sliver. The generator therefore checks every internal edge at the end and repairs bad ones: it flips the shared diagonal of two triangles where that helps, and otherwise emits the lattice square around the edge again in its canonical pattern. All of this works on integer lattice indices; only the measure uses coordinates. If invalid edges remain, OrthogonalityRepairError carries the raw mesh and their locations.
When refining, only edges next to new cells are judged: a mesh from another program may have edges that are not orthogonal by this measure (for example pentagon transition cells, whose centroid is off-centre), and refine does not fail on what it did not change.

title: Output contract: the same cells, compared on lattice indices
text: Two meshes are “the same” when they contain the same set of cells, with every node compared as an integer lattice index (in units of base cell / 2^L from the lattice origin, normalised to the finest level of both meshes). The order of cells and the numbering of nodes are free. Golden-master meshes from the generator at qgis_dhydamo 9a324bc guard this contract; any intended change to the cells a given input produces is a minor version or higher, with a changelog entry.

title: Output contract: the same cells, compared on lattice indices
text:
Considered Options

Bit-identical arrays, order included. Rejected: it blocks restructuring (vectorising, a different iteration order) without benefiting any caller. rooster_2d_verfijnen already compares cells independently of order.
Float coordinates with a tolerance. Rejected: a tolerance makes “equal” fuzzy, and float coordinates can differ in the last bit between runs when the base cell is not an exact binary fraction (e.g. 10.1 m) and the lattice origin differs.

title: Output contract: the same cells, compared on lattice indices
text:
Consequences

A cell is compared as a polygon: the node it starts with and its orientation are free. The generator at 9a324bc writes about 5% of its transition triangles clockwise; this package writes every face counterclockwise, and check reports the orientation separately.
Everything up to the final conversion works in integer lattice indices, including the centre nodes the orthogonality repair adds.
Dropping the old 1 m minimum cell size is an intended output change: a 24 m base cell asked for 5 levels now gives 0.75 m cells instead of being capped at 1.5 m.

title: Refine starts from the existing mesh; generate is refine of an empty base grid
text: Refining an existing refined quad mesh rebuilds the quadtree from the mesh’s own cells (squares as leaves, transition triangles as parts of their parent square) on a lattice derived from the mesh, adds the new refinement areas, re-balances only where needed and leaves all other cells exactly in place. Generating a new mesh is the same operation applied to the base grid covering the domain, so there is one engine and the property refine(generate(X), Y) == generate(X + Y) can be tested.

title: Refine starts from the existing mesh; generate is refine of an empty base grid
text:
Considered Options

Re-run the generator with the original input (the approach of rooster_2d_verfijnen in DHYDRO_Varianten: run twice in a window, without and with the new areas, and splice in the difference). Rejected: it needs the original generator input (config.ini) and only works for meshes this generator made with a lattice origin at a multiple of the base cell. It also fails for meshes made before 24-10-2026: the generator then rounded the base cell down to a power of 2 (25 m became 16 m), so re-running the recorded input now gives a different lattice.

title: Refine starts from the existing mesh; generate is refine of an empty base grid
text:
Consequences

Refine never grows the mesh: new cells only replace existing ones within the footprint. A domain or water areas given to refine only remove new cells. The property above therefore holds exactly when the same domain and water areas are used and Y does not reach cells that generate(X) removed for water or domain.
Meshes from other tools can be refined, as long as their cells are axis-aligned squares on one lattice (rectangles and rotated grids are out of scope for now).
The original generator input is no longer needed to refine a mesh.

title: Decisions
text:
Architectural decisions that are hard to reverse, surprising without context and the result of a real trade-off.

0001 — Refine starts from the existing mesh
0002 — Output contract: the same cells, compared on lattice indices

title: Why refine starts from the mesh
text:
Refining used to mean generating the mesh twice with the original input, once with and once without the new areas, and splicing in the difference. That needs the original input, works only for meshes this generator made on a lattice through a multiple of the base cell, and fails for models made before 24-10-2026, when the generator still rounded the base cell down to a power of 2 (25 m became 16 m).
refine starts from the mesh itself instead (ADR-0001):
generate is the same operation started from the base grid, which is why refine(generate(X), Y) gives the same cells as generate(X + Y) when the domain and the water areas are the same and Y stays away from where water or the domain removed cells.

title: Why refine starts from the mesh
text:
The footprint rule
The footprint is the area the cells of the mesh cover; holes are not part of it. Refining never adds cells outside it: new cells only replace existing ones. A domain or water areas given to refine only remove new cells.
A lattice square that its cells fill only partly — because cells were clipped along water — is recognised too. Untouched, it keeps its remaining cells. When it must become finer, a new cell in it stays only where it lies completely within the old cells, so the mesh does not grow into the water; where finer cells cannot fill a clipped triangle exactly, a little area is lost.

title: Why refine starts from the mesh
text:
Meshes from other programs
The lattice — origin, base cell and levels — is derived from the square cells, so any origin and any base cell work. Transition cells may follow any pattern (another triangulation, a pentagon) as long as the cells of a lattice square have their nodes only at its corners, side midpoints and centre. A square that is touched gets this package’s patterns; a square that is not keeps its own.

text:
Carry cell data over: the replacement map
result.replacement_map relates the new cells to the old ones:

source[i]: the old cell that new cell i lies in (for an unchanged cell, itself);
unchanged[i]: whether new cell i is an old cell with the same nodes;
removed: the old cells that are not in the new mesh.

)

text:
Domain and water areas
You may pass a domain and water areas to refine (or put them in the TOML file). They only remove new cells: existing cells stay. The domain’s holes are clipped like water. The mesh never grows: new cells only replace existing ones, inside the footprint of the mesh. See Why refine starts from the mesh.

title: Water areas
text: Water areas are where the 1D network carries the flow, so no 2D cells are kept there. Typically you refine along a watercourse and then cut the watercourse out: the small cells that remain follow its edge as closely as possible.

title: Water areas

A cell is removed when

NoteWhat MeshKernel does



MeshKernel keeps nodes and edges and derives the cells from them again. A single removed cell whose edges all stay (its neighbours all remain) therefore comes back, and a hole of three or four nodes becomes a cell again. That is accepted here, because it is what the models are built with; give bed levels as samples that are interpolated onto the cells rather than as values per cell.

title: generate
text:
generate(
    domain,
    *,
    cell_size,
    refinement_areas=(),
    transition_rows=1,
    water_areas=(),
    water_removal='centre',
    crs=None,
    origin=None,
    progress=None,
)
Generate a refined quad mesh over a domain.











Name
Type
Description
Default




domain
(shapely.Polygon, shapely.MultiPolygon, Areas or GeoDataFrame)
The area the mesh covers; its CRS is the CRS of the mesh and must be projected. A lattice square is kept whole when it overlaps the domain, so cells along the outer edge may reach slightly outside it. Holes in the domain are clipped like water areas, cell by cell, with the water removal rule.
required


cell_size
float
Side length of the base cell; any positive length.
required


refinement_areas
iterable of (shapely geometry, int), or Areas
Polygons (pairs, or :func:read_refinement_areas) paired with the refinement level their cells must reach (1 or higher); level L gives cells of cell_size / 2**L. The highest level among the areas is the highest level of the mesh.
()


transition_rows
int or sequence of int
Rows of finer cells kept around a finer area before the mesh coarsens, per step from coarse to fine: the first value is for the step from level 0 to 1. One value per level step, or a single value for every step; each at least 1.
1


water_areas
iterable of shapely geometry, Areas or GeoDataFrame
Polygons where no cells are kept, because the 1D network carries the flow there. Giving water areas applies them.
()


water_removal
('centre', 'inside', 'touches')
Water removal rule, applied cell by cell to the finished mesh, as clipping with MeshKernel does: a cell is removed when its circumcentre (triangle) or centroid lies in water ("centre", default, MeshKernel’s FACES_WITH_INCLUDED_CIRCUMCENTERS), only when it lies completely in water ("inside"), or as soon as it touches water ("touches"). The remaining small cells follow the water’s edge.
"centre"


crs
pyproj.CRS or str or int
CRS of input that carries none (shapely geometries). Input without CRS raises an error unless it is given; input with its own CRS is transformed to the CRS of the domain.
None


origin
tuple of float
A point of the lattice, so that the mesh lines up with an existing mesh or raster. By default the lower-left corner of the domain rounded down to a multiple of cell_size.
None


progress
callable
Called as progress(fraction, message) while the mesh is generated, with a fraction that rises from 0 to 1 and an English message. Returning True cancels the run.
None














Name
Type
Description





Mesh
The mesh in the CRS of the domain, its faces counterclockwise, on the lattice through origin.














Name
Type
Description





InputError
If input has no CRS and crs is not given, the CRS of the domain is geographic, the domain is empty or not polygonal, the cell size is not a positive length, a refinement area is empty or not polygonal, a level is not an integer of at least 1, the transition rows are not one integer of at least 1 per level step, a water area is empty or not polygonal, the water removal rule is unknown, the origin is not two finite numbers, or no cells are left inside the domain.



OrthogonalityRepairError
If the orthogonality repair cannot make every internal edge FM-orthogonal; it carries the raw mesh (mesh) and the problem locations (bad_points).



Cancelled
If the progress callback returned True.






>>> from shapely import Point, box
>>> mesh = generate(
...     box(0, 0, 400, 300),
...     cell_size=25.0,
...     refinement_areas=[(Point(200, 150).buffer(40), 2)],
...     transition_rows=[1, 1],
...     crs="EPSG:28992",
... )
>>> mesh.lattice.unit
6.25

The structure is that of the D-HYDRO mesh generator export: the Mesh2d topology with nodes, edges and faces, edge and face coordinates, face bounds, and node and face z set to -999 (no data) without a fill value, so readers do not mask them. A mesh with CRS EPSG:28992 gets exactly the CRS attributes of the D-Flow FM plugin; another CRS gets the same attributes derived with pyproj; a mesh without CRS gets no CRS variable.
